Second derivatives: forward over reverse

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-forward-reverse.Rmd
methods-forward-reverse.Rmd

cppODE() computes Hessian-vector products of a scalar functional by differentiating the reverse sweep in forward mode. Symbols are those of the notation table. R interface: derivMode = "forward-reverse" of cppODE() and cotangent, tangent and curvature of solveODE().

Hessian-vector products

For a fixed cotangent, Reverse (1) defines the gradient map \[ \bar\theta : \mathbb{R}^{M} \to \mathbb{R}^{M}, \qquad \theta \mapsto \nabla_\theta L(\theta), \tag{1} \] with Jacobian \(\nabla^2_\theta L\). The sweep evaluating (1) is generic in the scalar type. On \(\mathtt{dual}\langle\mathtt{double}\rangle\) with \(N\) tangent slots, seeded with \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}\), it returns the exact \((\nabla_\theta L,\; \nabla^2_\theta L\,V)\) [1]; \(V = I_M\) gives the Hessian. For an ODE this is the second-order adjoint [2], [3]. The result curvature, of shape \([n_x + n_p, N, n_{\text{seed}}]\), comes with the cotangent and tangent of the same run.

Second-order adjoint system

For a direction \(v = (v_0, v_p)\), the directional sensitivity \(\sigma\) solves Forward (1) contracted with \(v\), \[ \dot\sigma = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\sigma + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\,v_p, \qquad \sigma(t_0) = v_0, \tag{2} \] and the tangent \(\mu\) of \(\lambda\) along \(v\), the derivative of Reverse (2), runs backwards from \(\mu(T^+) = 0\), \[ \dot\mu_i = -\sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_i}\,\mu_k - \sum_k \lambda_k \left( \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j + \sum_m \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial p_m}\,v_m \right), \tag{3} \] with jumps \(\mu(t_o^-) = \mu(t_o^+) + \dot w_o\), \(\dot w_o\) the derivative of the cotangent row \(w_o\) along \(v\), zero for a cotangent independent of \(\theta\). A cotangent formed from the solution, such as a weighted residual, passes \(\dot w_o\) as the curvature argument, an array \([n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_x, n_{\mathrm{seed}}, N]\); without it the Hessian misses the dependence of the cotangent on \(\theta\), the gradient not. Differentiating Reverse (5) along \(v\) gives the state half \(\mu(t_0)\) of \(\nabla^2_\theta L\,v\) and the parameter half \[ \int_{t_0}^{T}\left( \sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial p_m}\,\mu_k + \sum_k \lambda_k \left( \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j + \sum_l \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial p_l}\,v_l \right)\right)\mathrm{d}t . \tag{4} \]

cppDE does not integrate (2) to (4); the dual instantiation gives their discrete counterpart. The tangent of \(\lambda\) is \(\mu\) on the forward grid, the tangent of the parameter accumulator is (4). The second derivatives of \(f\) in (3) and (4) come from \(J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) and \((\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) over duals, so the first-order sweep needs no further generated expression. For a Rosenbrock method these include the contractions of \(J v\), second derivatives of \(f\).

Cost and memory

The sweep reads tangents from the checkpoints, so the forward pass is a sensitivity run in the same \(N\) directions. A checkpoint holds \((q+1)\,n_x (N+1)\) numbers; memory is linear in the number of steps. The error test and first step of the forward pass include the tangents by sensErrCon (default TRUE); with sensErrCon = FALSE the grid does not depend on the directions. The cost, one sensitivity integration and one sweep of width \(N\), is linear in \(N\). A difference quotient of the gradient would cost \(N\) gradient evaluations and lose half the digits.

forward over forward forward over reverse
argument derivMode = "forward-forward" or deriv2 = TRUE derivMode = "forward-reverse"
result hessian: every state, every parameter pair Hessian of one functional
cost quadratic in \(M\) lower by a factor \(M\) for a likelihood
use state Hessians (only route); any functional by contraction Hessian of a likelihood

Linear solves and tangent storage

The matrix of a Rosenbrock stage has tangents, so the transposed solve applies the implicit function theorem with the transposed matrix (cppde_ad_lu.hpp dense, cppde_sparse_ad_lu.hpp sparse). The iteration matrix of a bdf or adams corrector has none: the sweep solves against it on values, with the tangents as further right-hand sides. A generated model body releases on return the tangent storage it allocated, so the sweep binds the tangent storage of every buffer before passing it to the model, as the stepper does for internal buffers.

References

[1]
B. A. Pearlmutter, “Fast exact multiplication by the Hessian,” Neural Computation, vol. 6, no. 1, pp. 147–160, 1994, doi: 10.1162/neco.1994.6.1.147.
[2]
Z. Wang, I. M. Navon, F. X. Le Dimet, and X. Zou, “The second order adjoint analysis: Theory and applications,” Meteorology and Atmospheric Physics, vol. 50, no. 1–3, pp. 3–20, 1992, doi: 10.1007/BF01025501.
[3]
D. B. Özyurt and P. I. Barton, “Cheap second order directional derivatives of stiff ODE embedded functionals,” SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing, vol. 26, no. 5, pp. 1725–1743, 2005, doi: 10.1137/030601582.
